a: they are the people I go to for advice
p: The Hebrew says God's decrees are "the men of my counsel"; the Greek puts "your rules" in the line.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: the men of my counsel
readings.plain: they are the people I go to for advice

readings.w: Old Greek: Rahlfs' text (checked on bibelkommentare.de) and Codex Sinaiticus (300s AD; checked in the Lake facsimile as transcribed on sourcelibrary.org), Psalm 118
readings.orig: καὶ αἱ συμβουλίαι μου τὰ δικαιώματά σου
readings.en: and my counsels are your rules
readings.plain: and my counsel is your rules

why: The Hebrew is the harder, more vivid reading: the decrees are like trusted advisers. The Greek gives the line one of the law words, perhaps by reading the phrase in light of the rest of the psalm.

a: your rulings I have placed in front of me
t: "I have set" or "I have not forgotten"?
p: The Hebrew says "your rulings I have set"; the Greek says "your rulings I have not forgotten".

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: your rulings I have set (before me)
readings.plain: your rulings I have placed in front of me

readings.w: Old Greek: Rahlfs' text (checked on bibelkommentare.de) and Codex Sinaiticus (300s AD; checked in the Lake facsimile as transcribed on sourcelibrary.org), Psalm 118; Gallican Latin iudicia tua non sum oblitus
readings.en: your judgments I have not forgotten
readings.plain: your rulings I have not forgotten

why: Shivviti, "I have set", is short and needs "before me" understood (compare 16:8, "I have set the LORD before me"). The Greek may have read a similar-looking verb (perhaps shakhachti, "I forgot", with a negative supplied) or smoothed the line with the psalm's frequent "I have not forgotten". The Hebrew is kept.

a: for I have hoped for your ruling
p: The Hebrew has "your ruling", singular; the Greek has "your judgments".

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: for your ruling
readings.plain: for I have hoped for your ruling

readings.w: Rahlfs' Greek text (checked on bibelkommentare.de), Psalm 118 (epi ta krimata sou); Codex Sinaiticus epi tois krimasin sou
readings.en: on your judgments I have hoped
readings.plain: for I have hoped in your rulings

why: The singular can mean God's verdict in the speaker's case, which fits a man waiting to be cleared. The Greek plural matches the rest of the psalm. The difference is one Hebrew letter (a yod).

a: toward your commands, the ones I love
p: "Which I love" repeats the end of 119:47. Many scholars think a copyist wrote it twice.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Rahlfs' Greek the same; Codex Sinaiticus adds "greatly"
readings.en: toward your commands, which I love
readings.plain: toward your commands, the ones I love

readings.w: Modern conjecture (no manuscript)
readings.en: toward your commands
readings.plain: toward your commands

why: Every witness has the phrase, so the Plain English Translation keeps it. The conjecture rests only on the verse's length and the repetition.

a: Their heart has gone dull like fat
p: The Hebrew says the heart is thick "like fat"; the Greek says "curdled like milk".

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: their heart is gross like fat
readings.plain: Their heart has gone dull like fat

readings.w: Old Greek: Rahlfs' text (checked on bibelkommentare.de) and Codex Sinaiticus (300s AD; checked in the Lake facsimile as transcribed on sourcelibrary.org), Psalm 118; Gallican Latin coagulatum est sicut lac cor eorum
readings.orig: ἐτυρώθη ὡς γάλα ἡ καρδία αὐτῶν
readings.en: their heart was curdled like milk
readings.plain: Their heart has curdled like milk

why: Hebrew chelev, "fat", and chalav, "milk", are spelled with the same three letters; only the vowels differ, and those were not written in early manuscripts. The Greek read "milk". A fat heart is a dull, unfeeling one (Isaiah 6:10), which fits the line, so the Hebrew vowels are kept.

a: and those who know your decrees
t: "Those who know" or "and they will know"?
p: The written Hebrew (Ketiv) has "and they will know"; the reading tradition (Qere) has "and those who know".

readings.w: Masoretic Text, Qere (the reading tradition); Greek kai hoi ginōskontes
readings.en: and those who know
readings.plain: and those who know your decrees

readings.w: Masoretic Text, Ketiv (the written consonants)
readings.en: and they will know
readings.plain: so that they will know your decrees

why: The Qere makes a neat pair, "those who fear you, those who know your decrees", and the Greek agrees. The Ketiv makes the second line the result: let them turn to me, so they will know. See the topic page on Ketiv and Qere.

a: The arrogant have dug pits for me
p: The Hebrew says the arrogant "dug pits"; the Greek says lawless men "told me idle tales".

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: the arrogant dug pits for me
readings.plain: The arrogant have dug pits for me

readings.w: Old Greek: Rahlfs' text (checked on bibelkommentare.de) and Codex Sinaiticus (300s AD; checked in the Lake facsimile as transcribed on sourcelibrary.org), Psalm 118
readings.en: lawless men told me idle talk
readings.plain: Lawless people have told me idle tales

why: Shichot, "pits", looks like sichot, "talk, musings" (the noun of the verb "ponder" in this psalm), and the Greek read it that way, also reading "dug" as "told". With "not in keeping with your law" the Greek makes a contrast between their talk and God's law. The Hebrew picture of traps fits 119:110 and is kept.

a: People of divided mind I hate
p: The Hebrew has "the divided"; the Greek has "lawbreakers".

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: divided ones I hate
readings.plain: People of divided mind I hate

readings.w: Old Greek: Rahlfs' text (checked on bibelkommentare.de) and Codex Sinaiticus (300s AD; checked in the Lake facsimile as transcribed on sourcelibrary.org), Psalm 118
readings.en: lawbreakers I hate
readings.plain: Lawbreakers I hate

why: The Greek translator chose a word that sets the line against "your law" in the second half. Se'afim is rare, and the Greek may be a guess from context. The Hebrew is kept.

a: Like slag you put an end to all the wicked of the earth
p: The Hebrew: God removes the wicked like slag. The Greek: "I counted all the sinners of the earth as transgressors".

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: dross: you have made all the wicked of the earth cease
readings.plain: Like slag you put an end to all the wicked of the earth

readings.w: Old Greek: Rahlfs' text (checked on bibelkommentare.de) and Codex Sinaiticus (300s AD; checked in the Lake facsimile as transcribed on sourcelibrary.org), Psalm 118
readings.orig: παραβαίνοντας ἐλογισάμην πάντας τοὺς ἁμαρτωλοὺς τῆς γῆς
readings.en: I counted all the sinners of the earth as transgressors
readings.plain: I have counted all the wicked of the earth as lawbreakers

why: The Greek seems to have read hishbatta, "you made cease", as chashavti, "I counted", and sigim, "dross", as a word from sug, "turn aside". Some scholars prefer "you count" (chashavta), which also gives good sense. The Plain English Translation keeps the Hebrew.

a: My body bristles with dread of you
t: "My flesh bristles" or "nail down my flesh"?
p: The Hebrew is a statement of fear; the Greek and Latin made it a request: "Pierce my flesh with fear of you".

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: my flesh bristles from dread of you
readings.plain: My body bristles with dread of you

readings.w: Old Greek: Rahlfs' text (checked on bibelkommentare.de) and Codex Sinaiticus (300s AD; checked in the Lake facsimile as transcribed on sourcelibrary.org), Psalm 118; Gallican Latin confige timore tuo carnes meas
readings.orig: καθήλωσον ἐκ τοῦ φόβου σου τὰς σάρκας μου
readings.en: nail down my flesh with fear of you
readings.plain: Nail my body down with dread of you

why: The Greek read the consonants smr as an imperative and connected them with masmer, "nail". The Latin form of this reading was much used by Christian writers on self-denial. The Hebrew picture matches Job 4:15 and is kept.

a: all your orders about everything are right
t: "All orders of everything" or "all your orders"?
p: The Hebrew "all orders of all" is odd. The Greek suggests "all your orders".

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: all orders of everything I count right
readings.plain: all your orders about everything are right

readings.w: Old Greek: Rahlfs' text (checked on bibelkommentare.de) and Codex Sinaiticus (300s AD; checked in the Lake facsimile as transcribed on sourcelibrary.org), Psalm 118; the Great Psalms Scroll (11QPs-a) is reported to read "your orders" (as reported in an English presentation of the published scroll texts (dssenglishbible.com); the DJD editions and photographs were not checked); followed by many modern versions
readings.orig: πρὸς πάσας τὰς ἐντολάς σου κατωρθούμην
readings.en: I kept straight by all your commandments
readings.plain: all your orders are right

why: The Greek (Rahlfs and Codex Sinaiticus agree) points to a Hebrew piqqudekha, "your orders", in place of piqqudei khol; the two differ by a letter or two. Many scholars adopt it. The Plain English Translation keeps the Hebrew, reading "of everything" as "in every matter".

a: for your word I wait in hope
p: The written Hebrew (Ketiv) has "your words"; the reading tradition (Qere) has "your word".

readings.w: Masoretic Text, Qere
readings.en: for your word
readings.plain: for your word I wait in hope

readings.w: Masoretic Text, Ketiv; Greek eis tous logous sou (Rahlfs and Codex Sinaiticus)
readings.en: for your words
readings.plain: for your words I wait in hope

why: Both are good Hebrew. The Plain English Translation follows the Qere, as the site usually does; the Greek agrees with the Ketiv.

a: Those who chase after vile plans
t: Pursuers of scheming, or my pursuers?
p: The Hebrew says "pursuers of scheming"; the Greek says "those who pursue me with lawlessness".

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: pursuers of scheming
readings.plain: Those who chase after vile plans

readings.w: Old Greek: Rahlfs' text (checked on bibelkommentare.de) and Codex Sinaiticus (300s AD; checked in the Lake facsimile as transcribed on sourcelibrary.org), Psalm 118; some Hebrew manuscripts are reported to read רֹדְפַי, "my pursuers" (not checked)
readings.en: those who pursue me with lawlessness
readings.plain: Those who chase me with vile plans

why: The two Hebrew forms differ only in one vowel letter. "My pursuers" fits 119:84, 157 and 161. The Plain English Translation keeps the Leningrad Codex.

a: it is your word my heart fears
p: The written Hebrew (Ketiv) has "your words"; the Qere has "your word".

readings.w: Masoretic Text, Qere
readings.en: and of your word
readings.plain: it is your word my heart fears

readings.w: Masoretic Text, Ketiv; Greek apo tōn logōn sou (Rahlfs and Codex Sinaiticus)
readings.en: and of your words
readings.plain: it is your words my heart fears

why: As in 119:147, the Plain English Translation follows the Qere, and the Greek agrees with the Ketiv.

a: in your way give me life
p: This is one of the verses without a law word. Some scholars think "by your word" stood here, but the scrolls as reported agree with the Hebrew.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Old Greek: Rahlfs' text (checked on bibelkommentare.de) and Codex Sinaiticus (300s AD; checked in the Lake facsimile as transcribed on sourcelibrary.org), Psalm 118 (en tē hodō sou); the Great Psalms Scroll (11QPs-a) and 4QPs-g, as reported in an English presentation of the published scroll texts (dssenglishbible.com); the DJD editions and photographs were not checked
readings.en: in your way
readings.plain: in your way give me life

readings.w: Conjecture by some scholars, to fit the pattern (not found in any witness checked for this page)
readings.en: by your word
readings.plain: by your word give me life

why: "In your way" is in the Leningrad Codex, in the Greek (Rahlfs and Codex Sinaiticus), and, as reported, in both Qumran scrolls that preserve the verse. "By your word" would give the verse a law word and match the refrain "give me life by your word" (119:25, 107). The two words look very alike in Hebrew script, but no witness checked for this page has it, so the Plain English Translation keeps the Hebrew.
b: The scroll readings here come from an English presentation of the published texts; the Hebrew of the scrolls was not seen.

a: in the smoke
p: The Hebrew has "in smoke"; the Greek has "in frost".

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); 11QPs-a, as reported in an English presentation of the published scroll texts (dssenglishbible.com); the DJD editions and photographs were not checked
readings.en: in smoke
readings.plain: in the smoke

readings.w: Old Greek: Rahlfs' text (checked on bibelkommentare.de) and Codex Sinaiticus (300s AD; checked in the Lake facsimile as transcribed on sourcelibrary.org), Psalm 118; Gallican Latin in pruina
readings.en: in frost
readings.plain: in the frost

why: Qitor means smoke (Genesis 19:28) and also the thick haze of frost or fog (148:8, where it stands beside snow). The Greek took the second sense. Either way the skin is spoiled and shrunken. The Plain English Translation gives the more common meaning.

a: your rules I have not forgotten
t: A law word traded for loyal love
p: The Great Psalms Scroll is reported to read "you made me like a skin" and "your loyal love I have not forgotten".

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Old Greek: Rahlfs' text (checked on bibelkommentare.de) and Codex Sinaiticus (300s AD; checked in the Lake facsimile as transcribed on sourcelibrary.org), Psalm 118 (ta dikaiōmata sou)
readings.en: your rules I have not forgotten
readings.plain: your rules I have not forgotten

readings.w: Great Psalms Scroll (11QPs-a), as reported in an English presentation of the published scroll texts (dssenglishbible.com); the DJD editions and photographs were not checked
readings.en: your loyal love I have not forgotten
readings.plain: your loyal love I have not forgotten

why: As reported, the scroll also has "you made me" for "I have become" in the first line. With "loyal love" the verse would have no law word at all, so the scroll does not support the idea that every verse once had one. The Masoretic Text and the Greek agree, and the Plain English Translation follows them.

a: Today they stand by your rulings
p: The Greek reads "by your ordinance the day continues".

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: by your rulings they stand today
readings.plain: Today they stand by your rulings

readings.w: Old Greek: Rahlfs' text (checked on bibelkommentare.de) and Codex Sinaiticus (300s AD; checked in the Lake facsimile as transcribed on sourcelibrary.org), Psalm 118
readings.orig: τῇ διατάξει σου διαμένει ἡ ἡμέρα
readings.en: by your ordinance the day continues
readings.plain: By your rulings the day stands firm

why: The Greek made hayyom, "today", the subject: the day itself lasts by God's order, in line with 119:90. In the Hebrew the subject is the heavens and earth of 119:89–90.

a: is your word
p: Codex Sinaiticus reads "your law is a lamp"; Rahlfs' Greek has "your word" with the Hebrew.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Rahlfs' Greek text (checked on bibelkommentare.de), Psalm 118 (ho logos sou)
readings.en: your word
readings.plain: is your word

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (checked in the Lake facsimile, Source Library transcription)
readings.en: your law
readings.plain: is your law

why: Sinaiticus probably echoes Proverbs 6:23, "the teaching is a light", or simply swaps one law word for another. The Hebrew and the main Greek text agree on "word".

a: LORD, give me life by your word
t: "Give me life" or "be gracious to me"?
p: The Great Psalms Scroll is reported to read "be gracious to me" here.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: LORD, give me life by your word
readings.plain: LORD, give me life by your word

readings.w: Great Psalms Scroll (11QPs-a), as reported in an English presentation of the published scroll texts (dssenglishbible.com); the DJD editions and photographs were not checked
readings.en: be gracious to me, LORD, by your word
readings.plain: LORD, be gracious to me by your word

why: "Be gracious to me" is the prayer of 119:29, 58 and 132; the scroll seems to have traded one familiar plea for another. The Plain English Translation follows the Masoretic Text.

a: My life is in my palm all the time
t: In my hand or in your hands?
p: The Hebrew and Rahlfs' Greek have "in my hand"; Codex Sinaiticus has "in your hands".

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Rahlfs' Greek text (checked on bibelkommentare.de), Psalm 118 (en tais chersin mou); Gallican Latin in manibus meis
readings.en: my soul is in my palm continually
readings.plain: My life is in my palm all the time

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (checked in the Lake facsimile, Source Library transcription)
readings.orig: ἡ ψυχή μου ἐν ταῖς χερσίν σου διὰ παντός
readings.en: my soul is in your hands continually
readings.plain: My life is in your hands all the time

why: The Hebrew idiom means risking one's life (Judges 12:3; 1 Samuel 19:5). Codex Sinaiticus turns it into trust, like 31:5, probably by a slip or a pious change in Greek copying; the main Greek text and the Latin agree with the Hebrew.

a: forever, to the last
t: To the end, or for a reward?
p: 'Eqev means "end" or "reward". The Greek takes "reward".

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: forever, to the end
readings.plain: forever, to the last

readings.w: Rahlfs' Greek text (checked on bibelkommentare.de), Psalm 118; Codex Sinaiticus adds dia pantos, "continually"
readings.en: forever, for the sake of a reward
readings.plain: forever, for a reward

why: The letters are the same; the difference is in how 'eqev is understood (see the note at 119:33). The Hebrew reading tradition and most translations take "to the end".

a: for their trickery is falsehood
p: The Greek reads "for their thought is unjust".

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: for their deceit is falsehood
readings.plain: for their trickery is falsehood

readings.w: Old Greek: Rahlfs' text (checked on bibelkommentare.de) and Codex Sinaiticus (300s AD; checked in the Lake facsimile as transcribed on sourcelibrary.org), Psalm 118
readings.en: for their thought is unjust
readings.plain: for their thinking is unjust

why: The Greek seems to have read tar'itam, "their thought" (a word known from Aramaic), for tarmitam, "their deceit"; some modern versions footnote it. The Hebrew is kept.

a: My zeal
t: My zeal, your zeal, or zeal for your house?
p: The Hebrew has "my zeal". The Greek tradition is split: Rahlfs' text has "zeal for your house" (from 69:9), Codex Sinaiticus "your zeal".

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: my zeal
readings.plain: My zeal

readings.w: Rahlfs' Greek text (checked on bibelkommentare.de), Psalm 118 and most Greek manuscripts as Rahlfs prints them
readings.en: the zeal of your house
readings.plain: Zeal for your house

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (checked in the Lake facsimile, Source Library transcription)
readings.en: your zeal
readings.plain: Your zeal

why: The main Greek text has borrowed the line from 69:9, "Zeal for your house has eaten me up" (John 2:17), so the Greek translators themselves heard Psalm 69 here. Sinaiticus' "your zeal" may be a shortened form of the same. The Hebrew "my zeal" fits the speaker's grief at enemies who forget God's words and is kept. In the second line Sinaiticus also has "your commands" where Rahlfs and the Hebrew have "your words".

a: every one of your commands is truth
p: Codex Sinaiticus reads "all your ways are truth"; Rahlfs' Greek has "commands" with the Hebrew.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Rahlfs' Greek text (checked on bibelkommentare.de), Psalm 118 (hai entolai sou)
readings.en: and all your commands are truth
readings.plain: every one of your commands is truth

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (checked in the Lake facsimile, Source Library transcription)
readings.en: all your ways are truth
readings.plain: every one of your ways is truth

why: One more case of a law word traded for a near-synonym in a single manuscript. The Hebrew and the main Greek text agree.

a: by your loyal love give me life
p: The Great Psalms Scroll is reported to read "by your word" here.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: by your loyal love give me life
readings.plain: by your loyal love give me life

readings.w: Great Psalms Scroll (11QPs-a), as reported in an English presentation of the published scroll texts (dssenglishbible.com); the DJD editions and photographs were not checked
readings.en: by your word give me life
readings.plain: by your word give me life

why: The scroll's reading gives the line a second law word and matches the refrain of 119:25 and 107. Where 119:83 loses a law word in the scroll, this verse gains one: the scroll does not push steadily toward the pattern. The Plain English Translation follows the Masoretic Text.
